extracted.intended_audience: authors of fiction, literary-community members, and general readers researching literary awards
extracted.subtask_description: Key facts and rules for the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction: who is eligible, how the award is described and administered, prize amounts, and historical/founding context. Useful for authors checking eligibility or researchers cataloging literary-prize criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award scope and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction is awarded annually by the PEN/Faulkner Foundation to the authors of the year's best works of fiction by living Americans, Green Card holders or permanent residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single sentence on the page combines the award's purpose (best works of fiction) with the stated eligibility pool (living Americans, Green Card holders, or permanent residents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: citizenship/residency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible authors must be living Americans, Green Card holders or permanent residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly limits eligibility to these categories; elsewhere the page links to discussion/coverage (e.g., Book Riot) about citizenship requirements and debates over whether such requirements are outdated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award frequency and inception
rubrics_metrics.description: The award is given annually; the award was first given in 1981.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: founded following the 1979 National Book Award controversy; Mary Lee Settle was one of the founders. Useful for understanding longevity and annual cadence of submissions/consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize amounts and distribution to finalists
rubrics_metrics.description: The winner receives US$15,000 and each of four runners-up receives US$5,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states the monetary awards and implies a five-finalist structure (one winner + four runners-up). This is a concrete procedural/award metric authors may care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of runners-up / finalist count
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of four runners-up receives US$5,000 (implying the typical finalist slate includes four runners-up plus one winner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly lists shortlists and winners; the explicit mention of four runners-up sets an expected finalist count and prize split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process: peer-juried
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization claims it to be 'the largest peer-juried award in the country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that selection is done by peer jurors (writers/peers) rather than by a commercial or purely editorial panel. The page also notes that judges read citations for each finalist at the presentation ceremony, indicating a juried deliberation and public citation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation ceremony practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges read citations for each of the finalists' works at the presentation ceremony in Washington, D.C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural detail describes part of the public award ritual and how finalists are formally presented and described at the ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founding ethos / rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The award was founded following the controversy at the 1979 National Book Award, when PEN America voted for a boycott on the grounds that the award had become too commercial; Mary Lee Settle was one of the founders of the PEN/Faulkner Award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page frames the award's origin as a response to perceived commercialism of other awards, suggesting an ethos valuing peer judgment and literary values rather than commercial considerations. This is contextual guidance about the award's standards and identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public record of winners and shortlists
rubrics_metrics.description: The article contains exhaustive lists of winners and shortlists by year from 1981 through recent years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not an evaluative criterion per se, the extensive winners/shortlist record functions as precedent for what the jurors have previously valued (genres, styles, notable authors) and can serve as a practical guide to the kind of work historically recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notion of 'best' left undefined
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are described as 'the year's best works of fiction' without a formalized, itemized set of literary-evaluation criteria on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page does not enumerate specific literary criteria (e.g., originality, prose style, thematic depth). Instead, 'best' is left to the peer-juried selection process and is implicitly guided by the judges' tastes and precedent as seen in past winners/shortlists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public discussion of eligibility norms
rubrics_metrics.description: The page references external discussion (e.g., 'Citizenship is an Outdated Requirement for Literary Prize Eligibility' - Book Riot) questioning the citizenship/residency eligibility requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that eligibility rules have been and may be subject to public debate and critique; applicants and observers should be aware that policies and community norms around eligibility can be contested and may evolve.
